prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange my preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part B045 prize to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The case rests on the science. Holst established incretin physiology and GLP-1 action in humans, Drucker defined proglucagon-derived peptide biology and receptor mechanism, and Mojsov identified the truncated active GLP-1(7-36) form that made a physiologically meaningful peptide therapy conceivable. The mechanism is confirmed by large independent outcome trials in glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal disease, so maturity is not in question. Six matching first-round configurations are not evidence of merit, and I have tested the trio against the alternatives raised, not only against the tally.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is still attribution. Four names are credited for three seats, Mojsov's priority over the active peptide form is contested with Habener, who is outside the supplied names, and I cannot settle that from the evidence in front of the committee. Excluding Knudsen means the prize stops short of the drug design that carried the discovery to patients, and a public reader may see that as an omission. The commercial scale of semaglutide and tirzepatide may also distort how original the underlying physiology looks. I accept these costs because a discovery prize should rest on the physiology and the identification of the active peptide, and the citation can state the therapeutic consequence without crediting drug development.

responses.point: Sandberg asks whether a two-part prize, for example GLP-1 reduced to two names plus the unfolded protein response (B015), would be better than a single three-name B045 prize.
responses.response: I considered this and decline it. Cutting B045 to two names would force out one of Holst, Drucker or Mojsov, each of whom has a distinct and necessary claim, in order to create room for a second part. That worsens the attribution problem that already troubles us. B015 has a clean credit to Walter and Mori and is conceptually elegant, as you say, but its disease link is still developing. I do not think a clearer second part justifies weakening the strongest achievement on the list. I keep B015 as a first-rank alternative, not as a partner to B045.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius treats B003 as the principal alternative, not a co-prize, because the Frazer and Zhou history and the parallel VLP work are unresolved, and notes that zur Hausen's prize covered viral aetiology, not VLP vaccine design.
responses.response: I agree that zur Hausen's prize should not count against B003 on novelty, and that adding B003 to B045 would exceed three laureates. I also agree that the Frazer and Zhou priority questions cannot be resolved from the supplied names. That is why B003 is my first fallback and not a co-recipient. It has the population-level cancer-prevention data that B015 lacks. If the committee cannot settle the Mojsov question for B045, B003 would be my first fallback, though its attribution risk is of the same kind, so it would be a replacement of one contested credit by another and not an escape from the problem.

responses.point: Perlmann says Mojsov's contested priority could be hard to defend publicly and that Knudsen should replace Mojsov if the citation is meant to cover the drugs as well as the physiology.
responses.response: I share the worry about defensibility, but I do not think it argues for Knudsen. My round-1 point stands: acylation was a real conceptual step, but it is the first step in drug development after the discovery and not part of the discovery that the citation names. A prize that credits Knudsen without Mojsov leaves the identification of the active peptide unrewarded, and Mojsov's contested priority is a risk we can state openly and not a reason to remove her. I would rather the citation say plainly that it concerns the physiology and the active peptide, so that the committee's reasoning is explicit and the exclusion of drug design is a stated choice, not an oversight.

responses.point: El-Manira moved from a Knudsen configuration to the Mojsov trio, and ranks optogenetics (B006) as an alternative, treating it as a methodological discovery of very broad use.
responses.response: Your move to the Mojsov trio matters to me, because it means the version with Knudsen no longer has support in any of the six configurations. I still do not share your view of B006 as a lead alternative. Its credit is spread across six names, and a three-person limit would exclude Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenböck without a principled basis. Sandberg, as you report, also sees it mainly as a research tool with limited clinical impact so far. I would put it behind B003 and B015, where the credited names are clearer.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contested priority for the active GLP-1 peptide against Habener, who is not among the credited names, is secure enough to carry a seat. I have not verified priority from primary documents.
How best to word the citation so it acknowledges the therapeutic consequence and Knudsen's role without crediting drug development.
Whether B003's Frazer and Zhou attribution questions could ever be settled well enough for it to be a real alternative.
Long-term safety and durability of GLP-1 therapies are still under study.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. My profile documents about twenty co-authored works with committee colleague Thomas Perlmann (dopamine neurons, Nurr1, autophagy), with no connection to any shortlisted candidate or credited name, so I see no need for recusal. I have a past Rockefeller link to Paul Greengard, who is not a candidate. No conflict with any credited name on the shortlist is apparent from my profile.
